title: Machine Learning for Fraud Detection in Digital Banking: A Systematic Literature Review
authors: George, M. Z. H.; Alam, M. K.; Hasan, M. T.
venue: ASRC Procedia: Global Perspectives in Science and Scholarship
tldr: Systematic review of 118 studies on ML fraud detection in digital banking, finding supervised learning dominant but deep learning emerging, with hybrid models showing superior adaptability.
problem_and_motivation: Digital banking fraud is a growing systemic risk yet detection research remains fragmented across methodologies, regions, and regulatory contexts. No comprehensive synthesis exists.
approach: Followed PRISMA guidelines with structured identification, screening, eligibility, and inclusion process.
Reviewed 118 peer-reviewed studies and institutional reports on ML fraud detection.
Analyzed supervised, unsupervised, deep learning, and hybrid model paradigms.
Compared cross-regional adoption patterns across EU, North America, and emerging economies.
Evaluated interpretability frameworks (SHAP, LIME) and evaluation metrics (precision, recall, F1, PR-AUC).
findings: Supervised learning (decision trees, logistic regression, SVM) remains dominant due to interpretability.
Deep learning (RNN, CNN, LSTM) transformative but faces interpretability and real-time deployment challenges.
Hybrid models combining supervised, unsupervised, and deep learning show superior detection accuracy.
EU emphasizes PSD2/GDPR compliance; North America leverages fintech partnerships; emerging economies face infrastructure gaps.
SHAP and LIME improve model transparency for regulatory acceptance.
Gaps remain in reproducibility, robustness under distributional shift, and criminological theory integration.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: Provides systematic synthesis of 118 studies on ML-based fraud detection. Maps methodological evolution from rule-based to hybrid deep learning systems. Identifies cross-regional regulatory and infrastructure variations affecting adoption.
directly_justifies: Supervised learning dominates but deep learning is emerging in fraud detection.
Hybrid models combining paradigms show superior adaptability.
SHAP and LIME enhance model transparency for regulatory compliance.
Gaps remain in reproducibility and distributional shift robustness.
limits: Review limited to studies published before search date; recent innovations may be excluded.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: Systematically scanned all domains. Assigned 4.A, 4.B, 8.B high relevance. Assigned 5.C, 10.A medium. Rejected demographic and budgeting topics as paper focuses on fraud detection technology.

limitations: Review limited to 118 studies; may miss emerging work. [unacknowledged]
No original empirical experiments or model comparisons.
Cross-regional analysis may oversimplify within-region variations.
remember_this: Supervised learning dominates; deep learning emerging for fraud detection.
Hybrid models show superior adaptability to evolving fraud tactics.
SHAP and LIME improve model transparency for regulators.
Cross-regional adoption varies by infrastructure and regulation.
Reproducibility and distributional shift robustness remain gaps.
